blocks.title: Barter and its problems
blocks.md: **Barter** is the exchange of goods for goods without money. Its problems: it needs a **double coincidence of wants** (each person must want what the other has); there is no common **measure of value**; goods may be **indivisible**; value cannot be easily **stored** (a goat may die); and **deferred payments** are hard to arrange. Money solves these problems.

blocks.title: Functions of money
blocks.md: Money is anything generally accepted as payment. Its functions: **medium of exchange** (used to buy and sell), **unit of account** (measures and compares values), **store of value** (keeps purchasing power for the future) and **standard of deferred payment** (debts and loans are fixed in money terms). In Cameroon the main money is the FCFA, issued by the central bank.

blocks.caption: A failed barter exchange: the farmer, the shoemaker and their different wants.
blocks.alt: Four boxes in a row showing the farmer with maize, wanting shoes, the shoemaker wanting fish and the failure of barter.

blocks.title: Qualities of good money
blocks.md: Good money is **acceptable** to everyone, **durable** (does not wear out), **portable**, **divisible** into small units, **scarce** enough to keep value, **uniform** (identical units) and **stable** in value. Forms of money: coins and notes, bank deposits (cheques, cards) and mobile money balances. **Legal tender** is money that the law says must be accepted for debts.

blocks.title: Money is not wealth
blocks.md: Money is a **means** of exchange, not the same as **wealth** (goods, land, skills). Printing more money does not make a country richer; it can cause **inflation**. A store of value can lose its worth if prices rise quickly. Do not write that money is the cause of all problems of exchange: banks and trust are also needed. Mobile money is a **form** of money, held on phone accounts.

blocks.title: Worked example — number of prices
blocks.statement: In a barter economy of 5 goods, every good must have a price in terms of each other good. How many exchange rates are needed? How many prices are needed if one good is chosen as money?
steps: With money, each of the 5 goods has one price; the money good has price 1 itself, so 4 prices are needed.
Money greatly reduces the number of prices to remember.
blocks.answer: 10 exchange rates in barter against 4 prices with money

blocks.title: Worked example — identify the function
blocks.statement: A trader in Garoua writes down that a goat costs 40 000 FCFA, keeps 20 000 FCFA in a drawer for next month, and pays for his goods by hand. Identify the functions of money shown.
steps: Stating the goat's price in FCFA is unit of account.
Keeping 20 000 for next month is store of value.
Paying for goods is medium of exchange.
blocks.answer: Unit of account; store of value; medium of exchange

blocks.title: Commercial banks
blocks.md: **Commercial banks** accept **deposits** (current and savings accounts), make **loans and overdrafts**, transfer money, change foreign currency and keep valuables safe. They earn profit mainly from the **interest margin**: they lend at a higher rate than they pay on deposits. They balance **liquidity** (cash ready for customers), **profitability** and **safety**. Simple interest: **I = P × r × t** (principal × rate × years).

blocks.title: BEAC and the CEMAC
blocks.md: The **CEMAC** (Central African Economic and Monetary Community) groups six countries: Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, the Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon. They share one currency, the **FCFA**, issued by the **BEAC** (Bank of Central African States), whose headquarters are in Yaoundé. The FCFA has a fixed rate with the euro (655.957 FCFA = 1 euro).

blocks.caption: A commercial bank sits between savers who deposit money and borrowers who take loans.
blocks.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows: savers, commercial bank, borrowers.

blocks.title: Functions of the central bank
blocks.md: A central bank **issues notes and coins**, is **banker to the government** and **to commercial banks**, holds the country's **reserves of foreign currency**, acts as **lender of last resort** and carries out **monetary policy** (managing the supply of money and interest rates) to keep prices stable. A separate regional body supervises commercial banks in the zone (COBAC).

blocks.title: Do not confuse banks
blocks.md: The BEAC serves banks and governments; ordinary people do not usually keep accounts there. A commercial bank cannot print FCFA. A fixed exchange rate gives stability but means a country cannot freely change its rate to help exports. Check carefully whether a question asks about the **zone** (CEMAC) or the **country** (Cameroon).

blocks.title: Worked example — bank margin
blocks.statement: A bank pays 4 % interest a year on deposits and charges 12 % on loans. It lends out 10 000 000 FCFA of deposits for a year (illustrative). Find the interest margin earned in FCFA.
steps: = 800000 FCFA before the bank's running costs.

blocks.title: Worked example — simple interest
blocks.statement: Manga borrows 500 000 FCFA at 10 % simple interest a year for 3 years (illustrative). How much will she repay in total?

blocks.title: Informal savings groups
blocks.md: A **njangi** (also called a **tontine**) is a **rotating savings and credit association**. Members meet regularly, each pays a fixed contribution, and the total (the **pot**) goes to one member in turn until everyone has received it. It needs **trust** and rules, usually has no interest, and helps people save for rent, school fees or business capital.

blocks.title: Microfinance and credit unions
blocks.md: **Microfinance institutions (MFIs)** offer small savings accounts and **small loans** to households and small traders who may find it hard to deal with a big bank. **Credit unions** are cooperatives owned by their members, who save and borrow among themselves. Both are usually licensed and supervised. Their loans often have higher interest rates and short terms because costs per small loan are high.

items.text: A njangi round: the pot goes to the next member

blocks.caption: A njangi round: members contribute and the pot goes to each member in turn.
blocks.alt: Five member boxes arranged in a circle with arrows showing the order in which they receive the pot.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
blocks.md: **Njangi**: quick, local, flexible, no collateral; but no legal protection, little interest earned, risk of default and fixed amounts. **MFIs/credit unions**: provide small loans, teach saving and may give training; but interest rates can be high, and borrowers may become over-indebted. **Commercial banks**: safer for large sums and wide services but need documents and collateral.

blocks.title: Facts to avoid
blocks.md: Do not say that all informal groups are illegal or all MFIs are cheap. Rules depend on the type of group and on the law of the time. The CEMAC zone has regional rules for microfinance, but you should not quote details in exams unless you are certain. Keep to the **economic role**: saving, borrowing and risk.

blocks.title: Worked example — the pot
blocks.statement: A njangi has 10 members who each pay 20000 FCFA at every meeting (illustrative). How much is the pot? How much does a member pay in total in a full round and how much does she receive?
steps: A member pays 20 000 at each of 10 meetings = 200000 FCFA.
She receives the pot once = 200 000 FCFA, so she earns no interest.

blocks.title: Worked example — cost of a small loan
blocks.statement: An MFI lends 100 000 FCFA for 6 months and charges 2 % interest per month on the original sum (illustrative). Find the total interest and the total to repay.
